A connection can only be started from the inside, since an unsolicited inbound packet matches nothing in the table; the NAT box holds per-flow state that a router was designed not to need; and the end-to-end assumption that an address means the same thing everywhere is broken, which is why protocols that carry addresses inside their own payloads need help to survive it.

annotations.text: Subnet numbers step by 32 because the last bit borrowed from the host part is worth 32.
172.16.0.0/12 covers 172.16 through 172.31 only. Twelve mask bits leave four free bits in the second octet, which is 16 through 31.
The port is half the key. Without rewriting it, two inside hosts that happened to pick the same source port could not be told apart on the way back.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill each blank with a single value.
checkpoint.template:
The private block 172.16.0.0/12 ends at ___
Splitting a /24 into /27 subnets borrows ___ bits
and therefore yields ___ subnets of ___ usable hosts each
checkpoint.explain: A /12 fixes the first four bits of the second octet, so that octet ranges over 16 to 31 and the block ends at 172.31.255.255 - the trap is assuming a private block runs to the end of its first octet. Going from /24 to /27 lengthens the prefix by three bits, which is $2^3 = 8$ subnets of $2^5 = 32$ addresses, and the reserved network and broadcast addresses leave 30 usable in each.

sections.title: Too many addresses to spend, and the last hop
sections.body:
**IPv6** exists for one reason: 32 bits is $2^{32}$, about four billion addresses, for a world with far more than four billion connected devices. An IPv6 address is 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons, which is roughly $3.4 \times 10^{38}$ addresses - enough that the design stops rationing them and hands every subnet a /64, leaving 64 bits for the interface identifier.

Two shortening rules make them writable. Leading zeros within a group are dropped, so `0db8` becomes `db8` and `0000` becomes `0`. Then **one** run of all-zero groups may be replaced by `::`. Only one, because two would be ambiguous - the reader reconstructs the address by counting how many groups are missing, and could not divide that count between two gaps.

Neither address family can put a packet on a wire by itself, because Ethernet does not know what an IP address is. **ARP** is the bridge. Having masked the destination and found it local, a host broadcasts an ARP request - who has this IP address, tell me - and the interface that owns it answers by unicast with its MAC address. The result is cached for a few minutes so that the broadcast is not repeated for every packet.

Two consequences of that caching are worth holding on to. A stale entry outlives the machine it describes, so replacing a network card can leave the rest of the segment talking to nobody until the entries expire. And if the destination is **not** local, the host resolves its default gateway instead - which is why a wrong mask breaks everything beyond the wire while leaving local traffic working perfectly.
sections.code:
2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329   full form, 8 groups of 16 bits
2001:db8:0:0:0:ff00:42:8329               leading zeros in a group dropped
2001:db8::ff00:42:8329                    one run of zero groups becomes ::

2001:db8:acad:1::/64    routing prefix 48 bits, subnet id 16, interface id 64
fe80::/10               link-local, valid only on the wire it was formed on

ARP, on the wire, before the first IP packet can leave the host:

  broadcast   who has 192.168.10.190?  tell 192.168.10.130
  unicast     192.168.10.190 is at 00:1b:44:11:3a:b7

annotations.text: Three zero groups collapse to ::. The reader restores them by counting: eight groups are required and five are written, so :: stands for three.
A /64 leaves 64 bits for the interface identifier - more host bits in one subnet than there are IPv4 addresses in the entire world.
The request must be a broadcast: the sender does not yet know the MAC address it is asking about, so it cannot address the question to anyone in particular.

checkpoint.prompt: Apply the IPv6 shortening rules, and then reverse them.

steps.label: fe80:0000:0000:0000:0202:b3ff:fe1e:8329 in shortest form
2001:db8:acad:1::a written out in full, all 8 groups of 4 digits
how many bits an IPv6 address has in total

checkpoint.explain: In the first address there are two runs of zero groups - a single 0000 and a run of three - and only one may become ::, so the rule takes the longer run and the shorter one stays written as the literal 0. In the second, the run of three leading zero groups collapses and 0202 loses its leading zero. Expanding is the same rules run backwards: pad every group to four digits and restore exactly as many zero groups as are needed to reach eight.

guided-practice.prompt: Convert between dotted quad and binary. Write each octet as eight bits.
guided-practice.explain: 144 is 128 + 16, so the top bit and the fourth bit of that octet are set: 10010000. 198 is 128 + 64 + 4 + 2 = 11000110. Working down the place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 and subtracting whenever the value fits is faster and less error-prone than repeated division by two, and it keeps the leading zeros visible.

guided-practice.prompt: Convert between prefix length and mask, and count what the prefix leaves behind.
guided-practice.template:
/20 as a dotted-quad mask is ___
255.255.255.192 as a prefix length is /___
A /28 subnet holds ___ addresses in total and ___ usable host addresses
guided-practice.explain: /20 is sixteen ones followed by four more, so the third octet is 11110000 = 240 and the fourth is zero. 192 is 11000000, two ones, which added to the 24 before them makes /26. A /28 leaves four host bits: $2^4 = 16$ addresses, minus the network and broadcast addresses, so 14 usable. Answering 16 for both is the standard slip - the total and the usable count are never the same number.

steps.label: mask as a dotted quad
network address
broadcast address
first usable host address
last usable host address
number of usable host addresses

guided-practice.explain: A /28 makes the last octet step in sixteens, so the subnet containing 37 runs from 32 to 47. Clearing the four host bits of 00100101 gives 00100000 = 32, and setting them gives 00101111 = 47. Answering 192.0.2.37 for the network address is the usual error: an address is its own network address only when its host bits already happen to be zero.

guided-practice.prompt: A host with address `192.168.10.130/26` has an IP packet for `192.168.10.190` and an empty ARP cache. Put the steps in the order they happen.
fragments: The host ANDs the destination address with its own mask, and finds the result equals its own network address, so the destination is local.
Finding no entry, the host broadcasts an ARP request to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff asking who owns 192.168.10.190.
The host looks in its ARP cache for a mapping from 192.168.10.190 to a MAC address.
The owner of the address replies by unicast, giving its MAC address.
The host stores the mapping in its cache and sends the frame to that MAC address.
guided-practice.explain: The masking decision comes first and settles who is being asked about at all: local means ARP for the destination itself, remote means ARP for the default gateway instead. The cache is consulted before the broadcast because avoiding that broadcast is the entire purpose of the cache, and the reply is unicast because by then the responder knows exactly who asked.

address-arithmetic.prompt: An interface is configured `192.168.10.130/26`. Work out every figure below.

steps.label: mask as a dotted quad
network address
broadcast address
first usable host address
last usable host address
number of usable host addresses
is 192.168.10.190 reachable without a router - yes or no

address-arithmetic.explain: A /26 leaves six host bits, so the last octet moves in blocks of 64 and 130 falls in the block 128 to 191. That gives .128 as the network address, .191 as the broadcast address and $2^6 - 2 = 62$ usable addresses from .129 to .190. Since .190 masks to the same .128 network it is a direct neighbour and needs no router - the tempting wrong answer is no, on the reasoning that .130 and .190 look far apart, but sixty apart is nothing next to a 64-address block.

address-arithmetic.prompt: Two interfaces at different sites: `10.1.200.75/20` and `172.20.144.19/22`. Report the figures for each.

steps.label: 10.1.200.75/20 network address
10.1.200.75/20 broadcast address
10.1.200.75/20 number of usable host addresses
172.20.144.19/22 network address
172.20.144.19/22 broadcast address
172.20.144.19/22 last usable host address

address-arithmetic.explain: When the boundary falls inside the third octet the whole fourth octet is host bits, which is why both broadcast addresses end in 255. A /20 leaves four free bits in the third octet, so subnets step in sixteens and 200 sits in the block 192 to 207; a /22 leaves two, so they step in fours and 144 begins a block ending at 147. The host counts are $2^{12} - 2 = 4094$ and $2^{10} - 2 = 1022$. Treating 10.1.207.255 as an ordinary host address is the mistake to avoid: it is the broadcast address of that subnet and cannot be assigned, even though it does not sit at the end of an obvious boundary.

address-arithmetic.prompt: You are given the public block `203.0.113.0/24` and asked to cut it into equal /27 subnets.

steps.label: number of bits borrowed from the host part
number of subnets produced
mask of each subnet as a dotted quad
usable host addresses per subnet
network address of the third subnet, counting the lowest as the first
broadcast address of that third subnet
network address of the subnet containing 203.0.113.150

address-arithmetic.explain: Lengthening the prefix from 24 to 27 borrows three bits, giving $2^3 = 8$ subnets of $2^5 = 32$ addresses and 30 usable in each. The subnets therefore begin at multiples of 32, so the third runs .64 to .95, and 150 lands in the block .128 to .159. Off-by-one on the third subnet is the classic slip: the first subnet is .0, not .32, because the block starts at zero.

address-arithmetic.prompt: For each pair, decide whether the two addresses are on the **same** subnet or on **different** subnets, using the prefix given.

steps.label: 10.1.200.75/20 and 10.1.208.4 - same or different
role of 172.20.147.255 in that subnet - host or broadcast

address-arithmetic.explain: The test is always the same: mask both addresses and compare the results. .190 and .130 both mask to 192.168.10.128, while .200 masks to 192.168.10.192 and is a different subnet despite lying only ten above a member of the first. 10.1.208.4 masks to 10.1.208.0, one /20 above 10.1.192.0. The last pair is the trap worth meeting: 172.20.147.255 does mask to 172.20.144.0 and so is on the subnet, but it is that subnet's broadcast address and no host may hold it - membership and assignability are separate questions.

address-arithmetic.prompt: Work with IPv6 addresses and their shortening rules.

steps.label: number of bits left for the interface identifier in a /64
number of /64 subnets inside a /48 site prefix
how many times :: may appear in one address

address-arithmetic.explain: The second address has two runs of zero groups, but the rule allows one :: only, so the longer leading run collapses and the trailing zeros stay written out as 0:0. Between /48 and /64 lie sixteen bits, giving $2^{16} = 65536$ subnets, and a /64 leaves 64 interface bits by design so that stateless address autoconfiguration always has room. Writing 2001:db8::1::1 is the tempting answer and is not an address at all: a reader could not tell how to divide the missing groups between the two gaps.

network-diagnosis.prompt: A site uses `10.1.192.0/20` on one flat segment, with its router at `10.1.192.1`. A newly installed server is configured with address `10.1.200.75`, mask `255.255.255.0` and gateway `10.1.192.1`. It can ping `10.1.200.9` and `10.1.200.240` perfectly, but nothing outside 10.1.200.x at all, and its ARP cache holds no entry for the router. Name the cause and explain the exact mechanism.
network-diagnosis.answer: The server's subnet mask is too long - a /24 where the segment is a /20 - so it believes its own default gateway is on a different subnet and never resolves it
network-diagnosis.explain: With a /24 mask the server computes its own network as 10.1.200.0 and masks 10.1.192.1 down to 10.1.192.0, a different network, so the gateway looks remote. A host only ever resolves the link-layer address of something it believes is local, so it sends nothing anybody on the wire will answer and the cache stays empty; with no gateway it can reach, everything off the segment fails. The symptom pattern is the giveaway, and it is also the reason the wrong diagnosis tempts: local traffic within 10.1.200.x works flawlessly because those addresses really are local under either mask, which makes the cabling and the switch look innocent, as they are.

network-diagnosis.prompt: A failed server is replaced by an identical machine keeping the same IP address `192.168.10.190`, but carrying a new network card and so a new MAC address. The router reaches it immediately. Other hosts on the same segment cannot reach it at all, then begin to succeed one by one over the next few minutes with nobody doing anything. Name the cause and explain the mechanism.
network-diagnosis.answer: Stale ARP cache entries on the other hosts still map 192.168.10.190 to the old card's MAC address, and only recover as those entries time out
network-diagnosis.explain: Resolution is cached precisely so that the broadcast is not repeated for every packet, and the price of that cache is that it describes the world as it was when the entry was made. Frames are still being addressed to a MAC address that no longer exists on the segment, so they are delivered nowhere and nothing reports an error - which is why the failure is silent rather than a refusal. Recovery one host at a time is the signature of independent expiry timers, and the router recovered first simply because its own entry happened to lapse or be refreshed sooner; a gratuitous ARP from the new card would have overwritten every cache at once.

network-diagnosis.prompt: A small office runs about 40 machines on `192.168.1.0/24` behind a single broadband connection with one public address. Explain what has to happen to a packet sent from `192.168.1.7` to a web server at `93.184.216.34` port 443, on the way out and on the way back. Then explain why a colleague who wants to run a game server on their desktop cannot simply give people its address.
network-diagnosis.explain: 192.168.1.7 comes from a private block that no Internet router will carry, so a reply addressed to it could never come back; the NAT box therefore rewrites the source address to its own public address and the source port to a value it can keep unique, records the mapping, and reverses the rewrite on every reply that matches an entry. The inbound case fails for exactly the reason the outbound one works: the entry is created by the packet leaving, so an unsolicited packet arriving for the game server matches nothing and is dropped. The tempting answer is that the address is merely hidden and could be published - the point is stronger than that, because the address is not unique in the world and means something different inside every other office using the same block.

network-diagnosis.prompt: You are given the private block `192.168.20.0/24` for a single site with four segments: an office of about 100 machines, a lab of about 50, a wireless guest network of about 25, and two point-to-point router links carrying two addresses each. Produce an address plan. For each segment give the prefix you chose and why, the network and broadcast addresses it implies, and the usable host range. Then say what headroom is left for growth, and what would change if the site were addressed from an IPv6 /48 instead.
network-diagnosis.explain: Sizing runs downwards from the largest requirement. 100 machines need seven host bits, so a /25 at 192.168.20.0 with broadcast .127 and hosts .1 to .126; 50 need a /26 at .128 with broadcast .191 and hosts .129 to .190; 25 need a /27 at .192 with broadcast .223 and hosts .193 to .222; and each router link needs exactly two addresses, which is a /30, so .224/30 and .228/30 with usable pairs .225 to .226 and .229 to .230. That leaves only .232 to .255 - a spare /29 and /30 - which is the honest lesson of variable-length subnetting: fitting the requirements exactly is possible and leaves almost nothing over, so a plan that expects the lab to double should take a /25 for it now rather than a /26. Allocating four equal subnets instead is the tempting simplification, and four /26s cannot be made to work at all, because the office needs more than the 62 hosts a /26 provides. From an IPv6 /48 the arithmetic disappears: every segment takes a /64 whatever its size, 65536 of them are available, the point-to-point links get one each without embarrassment, and no translation is needed because the addresses are globally routable.

exam.prompt: Which of these is **not** part of the RFC 1918 private address space?
exam.explain: The private range in the 172 space is a /12, which covers 172.16.0.0 through 172.31.255.255 only, so 172.40.x.x is ordinary public space belonging to somebody. It tempts because it begins with 172, and people remember the block by its first octet rather than by its prefix length.

exam.prompt: Which of the following are true of IPv6 addressing?
choices: An address is 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits
The `::` abbreviation may appear at most once in an address
Leading zeros within a group may be omitted
A subnet is conventionally a /64, leaving 64 bits of interface identifier
NAT is required for an IPv6 host to reach the Internet
exam.explain: The first four together are the whole notation and the standard subnet size. The last is false, and is precisely the habit IPv6 was meant to end: translation was a response to address scarcity, and with $2^{128}$ addresses a host can hold a globally routable one of its own. Sites still filter inbound traffic at a firewall, but that is a policy decision rather than an addressing necessity.

exam.prompt: Fill each blank with a single value.
exam.template:
/22 as a dotted-quad mask is ___
255.255.255.224 as a prefix length is /___
A /29 subnet has ___ usable host addresses
A /30 subnet has ___ usable host addresses
exam.explain: /22 is sixteen ones plus six more, so the third octet is 11111100 = 252. 224 is 11100000, three ones on top of the first 24, giving /27. The host counts are $2^3 - 2 = 6$ and $2^2 - 2 = 2$, and the second is why a /30 is the traditional size for a router-to-router link: it is the smallest block with anything usable left once the network and broadcast addresses are taken.

exam.prompt: Put the steps of deriving a subnet's boundaries from an address and a prefix into order.
fragments: Write the address and the mask in binary, one above the other.
Set every host bit to one to obtain the broadcast address.
Set every host bit to zero to obtain the network address.
Split the 32 bits at the prefix length: the bits above it are network bits, the bits below it are host bits.
Take everything strictly between those two addresses as the usable host range.
exam.explain: Everything after the split is mechanical, which is why the split is the step that has to come first and the one worth slowing down for. The network and broadcast addresses could be produced in either order, since neither depends on the other, but the usable range is defined by both and must come last - and it is strictly between them, never inclusive of them.

steps.label: mask as a dotted quad
network address
broadcast address
number of usable host addresses

exam.explain: A /29 leaves three host bits, so subnets step in eights and 201 sits in the block 200 to 207. Clearing the low three bits of 11001001 gives 11001000 = 200, and setting them gives 11001111 = 207, leaving .201 through .206 as the six usable addresses. Note that .201 happens to be the first usable address here, which is where it fell in the block rather than any rule about the address you were given.

exam.prompt: Two interfaces you have not seen before: `198.51.100.94/27` and `192.168.100.17/28`.

steps.label: 198.51.100.94/27 network address
198.51.100.94/27 broadcast address
198.51.100.94/27 last usable host address
192.168.100.17/28 network address
192.168.100.17/28 broadcast address
192.168.100.17/28 number of usable host addresses

exam.explain: A /27 steps in thirty-twos, so 94 lies in .64 to .95 and is the very last usable address, one below the broadcast - an address landing on an awkward-looking number is not evidence of a misconfiguration. A /28 steps in sixteens, putting 17 in .16 to .31 with .16 as the network address and $2^4 - 2 = 14$ usable. Reading 198.51.100.94 as the broadcast address is the error the shape of the number invites; the broadcast is .95.

exam.prompt: A block of `10.4.0.0/16` is to be divided into equal /22 subnets, one per branch office.

steps.label: number of subnets produced
mask of each subnet as a dotted quad
usable host addresses per subnet
network address of the second subnet, counting the lowest as the first
broadcast address of the subnet containing 10.4.13.200

exam.explain: Six bits are borrowed going from /16 to /22, giving $2^6 = 64$ subnets whose third octets step in fours, so they begin at 10.4.0.0, 10.4.4.0, 10.4.8.0 and so on. Each holds $2^{10} = 1024$ addresses and 1022 usable. 10.4.13.200 falls in the block beginning 10.4.12.0, whose broadcast is 10.4.15.255 - the trap is stopping at 10.4.13.255, which is merely the end of one octet inside a subnet four times that wide.

exam.prompt: Explain why the network address and the broadcast address of a subnet cannot be given to a host, and what that reservation costs as subnets get small. Use a /29 and a /30 to make the cost concrete.
exam.explain: The two addresses are reserved because they already mean something else: the all-zeros host pattern names the subnet itself, which is what a routing table entry refers to, and the all-ones pattern addresses every interface on it at once. The cost is a fixed two addresses whatever the subnet size, so it is invisible in a /16 and enormous in a /29, where six of eight survive, or a /30, where two of four do. The reasoning to resist is that the reservation is arbitrary bookkeeping that could simply be dropped - it could not, without losing any way to name a network as distinct from a host on it, which is why relaxing it for point-to-point links needed a deliberate change of rule rather than an author ignoring the convention.

exam.prompt: A LAN is `192.168.10.128/26` with its router at `192.168.10.129`. A workstation is statically configured with address `192.168.10.200`, mask `255.255.255.192` and gateway `192.168.10.129`. It reaches nothing at all - not the router, not any other machine on the wire - although its link light is on and the switch port shows traffic. Name the cause and explain the mechanism.
exam.answer: The workstation's address 192.168.10.200 lies in 192.168.10.192/26, not in the LAN's 192.168.10.128/26, so every destination including its own gateway looks remote to it
exam.explain: The mask is right and the gateway is right; the address itself is in the wrong block, because /26 boundaries fall every 64 addresses and 200 belongs to the block starting at 192, not the one starting at 128. Masking the gateway 192.168.10.129 gives 192.168.10.128, which does not match the workstation's own 192.168.10.192, so it treats even the router as remote and tries to reach it via a gateway it cannot resolve, sending ARP requests nobody on that wire will answer. Blaming the mask is the natural first move, because a right-mask-wrong-address fault presents identically to a wrong-mask fault from the console, and only writing both addresses out in binary separates them.

sections.title: The datagram, field by field
sections.body:
IP promises very little on purpose. A **datagram** is handed to the network with a destination address on it and no guarantee that it will arrive, arrive once, or arrive in order - and because IP promises so little, almost any link technology can carry it. Every field in the twenty-byte header exists to make that weak promise work across machines that agree on nothing else, so it is worth knowing what each one buys.

`Version` and `IHL` say how to parse the rest: `IHL` counts 32-bit words, so its minimum of 5 means the usual 20-byte header and its maximum of 15 means 60 bytes with options. `Total Length` is 16 bits and counts header **plus** payload, capping a datagram at 65,535 bytes. `Protocol` is the demultiplexing key for the layer above - 1 for ICMP, 6 for TCP, 17 for UDP - and the `Header Checksum` covers the header alone, never the data, which is why a corrupt payload is the transport layer's problem and not IP's.

**TTL** is a hop count, not a time. Every router decrements it and discards the datagram when it reaches zero, which is the only thing standing between a transient routing loop and a packet that circulates forever. It costs something: because TTL changes at every hop, the header checksum must be recomputed at every hop too, and that is one reason IPv6 dropped the header checksum entirely.

When the next link's **MTU** is smaller than the datagram, a router may **fragment** it. The payload is cut at 8-byte boundaries, each piece gets a copy of the header, the `Identification` field is copied so the pieces can be matched up, `Fragment Offset` records where the piece starts in units of 8 bytes, and the `MF` flag is set on every piece but the last. Reassembly happens **only at the destination**, because the pieces may take different routes - and since losing any one fragment destroys the whole datagram, modern senders set `DF` and discover the path MTU instead.

annotations.text: Version and IHL share the first byte. IHL counts 4-byte words, so the smallest legal value, 5, describes this 20-byte header.
Flags and Fragment Offset share a 16-bit field: three flag bits then thirteen offset bits. That is why the offset counts 8-byte blocks - thirteen bits times eight still reaches 65,528.
TTL and Protocol sit next to each other in one 16-bit word, which is what makes the incremental checksum update on a TTL decrement so cheap.
0x4000 is binary 010 in the flag bits: reserved 0, DF 1, MF 0. This datagram must not be fragmented, and it is not itself a fragment.

checkpoint.prompt: Read the four values straight out of the header above. Give the last one as a protocol name.
checkpoint.template:
An IHL of 5 describes a header of ___ bytes.
A Total Length of 60 therefore leaves ___ bytes of payload.
A fragment whose offset field reads 69 begins at byte ___ of the original payload.
A Protocol field of 6 means the payload is ___.
checkpoint.explain: IHL counts 32-bit words, so 5 words is 20 bytes; Total Length counts the header as well, so the payload is 60 - 20 = 40. The offset is in 8-byte units, so 69 means 69 x 8 = 552 bytes in - forgetting that multiplier is the commonest fragmentation error, and it makes every offset look eight times too small.

sections.title: Forwarding is not routing
sections.body:
Two different jobs get muddled under one word. **Forwarding** is what a router does to a datagram that has just arrived: look the destination up in a local table, decrement the TTL, send it out of an interface. It happens per packet, in hardware, in microseconds, and it involves no other router. **Routing** is the background conversation between routers that builds and maintains that table; it happens on a timescale of seconds and involves everybody. A router can forward perfectly well for minutes on a table whose routing protocol has died - it will simply be forwarding down paths that no longer exist.

The table is keyed by **prefixes**, not addresses. An entry like `10.20.64.0/18` names the addresses whose first 18 bits match, and maps all of them to one next hop. Entries overlap deliberately: an operator aggregates a whole region into one short prefix and then adds longer prefixes as exceptions for the parts that go somewhere else. Aggregation is what keeps the global table in the hundreds of thousands of entries rather than in the billions.

Overlap forces a tie-break, and the rule is **longest-prefix match**: among all entries that match, take the one with the most bits of prefix. It is the right rule because a longer prefix is a more specific statement about where those addresses are, and a specific statement should beat a general one. The default route `0.0.0.0/0` matches everything and, having zero prefix bits, always loses to any other match - which is exactly why it works as a catch-all rather than as a black hole. The cost is that a lookup is no longer an exact-match hash: the router must search across prefix lengths, which is why real hardware uses tries and TCAMs.
sections.code:
Forwarding table on router R1. The longest matching prefix wins.

  prefix              next hop        interface
  0.0.0.0/0           203.0.113.1     eth0      (the default route)
  10.0.0.0/8          direct          eth1
  10.20.0.0/16        10.0.0.9        eth2
  10.20.64.0/18       10.0.0.17       eth3
  10.20.96.0/19       10.0.0.33       eth4
  192.168.4.0/24      10.0.0.41       eth5
  192.168.4.128/26    10.0.0.49       eth6

/* The rule, stated exactly: every entry whose prefix matches is a
   candidate, and the candidate with the most 1 bits in its mask wins. */
struct entry *lookup(uint32_t dst)
{
    struct entry *best = NULL;

    for (struct entry *e = table; e; e = e->next)
        if ((dst & e->mask) == e->prefix)          /* a match */
            if (!best || e->len > best->len)       /* a longer one */
                best = e;

    return best;            /* NULL only if there is no default route */
}

/* What R1 does to one datagram, in order:
     1. verify the header checksum; discard silently if it fails
     2. look up the destination, longest prefix wins
     3. decrement TTL; if it is now zero, discard and send ICMP Time Exceeded
     4. fragment if the outgoing MTU is too small and DF is clear
     5. recompute the header checksum, because TTL and length may have changed
     6. hand the datagram to the outgoing link */

annotations.text: `direct` means the destination sits on a network R1 is attached to, so there is no next-hop router - R1 resolves the address on the link itself.
Note the two nested tests. Matching is not enough; the loop keeps searching for a longer match, and only the length decides. Nothing about table order matters.
The checksum is verified before anything changes and recomputed after everything has changed. Both steps are needed because the router itself modifies the header.

checkpoint.prompt: Look each destination up in R1's table above and name the outgoing interface.
checkpoint.explain: 10.20.100.7 matches four entries and the /19 is the longest, so eth4. 10.20.80.5 falls inside 10.20.64.0/18 but not inside 10.20.96.0/19, which only begins at 10.20.96.0, so the /18 wins and it leaves by eth3. 172.16.5.1 matches nothing but the default. Reading the table top to bottom and stopping at the first match would send the first two out of eth1, and that is the habit to break: position in the table means nothing at all.

sections.title: Two ways to fill the table
sections.body:
**Distance vector** asks each router to know almost nothing. It stores one number per destination - the cost - plus the neighbour it would send to, and periodically tells its neighbours that vector of costs. On hearing a neighbour's vector it re-runs Bellman-Ford: my cost to `d` is the cheapest of `cost to that neighbour + that neighbour's cost to d`. No router ever sees the topology, which makes the protocol cheap in memory and cheap to implement.

It pays for that ignorance with **count-to-infinity**. Good news spreads in one exchange; bad news crawls, because a router cannot tell that a neighbour's advertised route runs back through itself. When the link to X fails, Y hears Z still claiming a cost of 2 to X, adopts 3, Z then adopts 4, and the pair climb by one each exchange while bouncing X's traffic back and forth between them. The cures are all partial: a small finite **infinity** (RIP uses 16) bounds how long the climb lasts, and **split horizon** - never advertise a route back to the neighbour you learned it from, or advertise it as infinity, which is **poison reverse** - kills the two-router version outright. Neither kills a loop that runs round three or more routers, because then nobody is advertising a route straight back to its source.

**Link state** takes the opposite bet: flood everything, compute locally. Each router builds a link-state packet naming its neighbours and the cost to each, stamps it with a sequence number, and floods it out of every interface but the one it arrived on; each receiver stores it if the sequence number is newer and passes it on. When the flooding settles, every router holds the same map, and each independently runs **Dijkstra** on that map rooted at itself. The forwarding table is then just the first hop of each branch of the resulting shortest-path tree. The cost is real - every router stores the whole topology and recomputes on every change - which is precisely why OSPF cuts a large domain into **areas**, so that flooding and recomputation stop at the boundary.
sections.code:
/* Distance vector: Bellman-Ford, re-run on every advertisement received.
   A router knows only its own links and what its neighbours claim. */
for each destination d:
    D(x, d) = min over neighbours n of ( c(x, n) + D(n, d) )

X --1-- Y --1-- Z        all routes to X; then the X-Y link fails

  exchange   Y's cost to X   Z's cost to X   why
    start          1               2         converged and correct
      1            3               2         Y believes Z's stale 2
      2            3               4         Z hears Y's new 3
      3            5               4         Y hears Z's new 4
      4            5               6         and so on, by one each time
     14           15              16         16 is RIP's infinity: unreachable

  With split horizon at Z, Z never mentions X to Y at all, so at
  exchange 1 Y has nothing to fall back on and goes straight to 16.

/* Link state: everybody floods, then everybody computes alone. */
Dijkstra(source s):
    Confirmed = { s }, Tentative = { }
    repeat:
        for each neighbour n of the node just confirmed:
            offer (cost so far + link cost) into Tentative, keeping the best
        move the cheapest entry in Tentative into Confirmed
    until Tentative is empty

annotations.text: The whole protocol is this one line. Everything else - timers, poisoning, split horizon - exists to stop it converging on a wrong answer.
Y's new cost of 3 is a route through Z, and Z's route to X is through Y. Neither can see the loop, because neither can see anything but a number.
Confirmed grows by exactly one node per iteration, and a node's cost is final the moment it is confirmed - which is why a negative link cost would break the algorithm outright.

checkpoint.prompt: The three-router line `X --1-- Y --1-- Z` has converged on routes to X when the `X-Y` link fails. Split horizon is off. Report the costs to X as the exchanges go by.

steps.label: Y's cost to X after exchange 1
Y's next hop to X at that moment
Z's cost to X after exchange 2
the value at which RIP calls X unreachable

checkpoint.explain: Y loses its direct route and takes the only advertisement it has, Z's stale cost of 2, giving 1 + 2 = 3 through Z - which is a route running back through Y itself. From there each exchange adds one, so the pair climb together until they hit RIP's deliberately tiny infinity of 16. Expecting Y to jump straight to unreachable is the natural guess, and it is exactly what split horizon would produce; without it Y has no way to learn that Z's route is its own.

sections.title: Inside, outside, and the probes that show you the path
sections.body:
The Internet is not one routing domain. It is roughly a hundred thousand **autonomous systems**, each independently administered and free to run whatever routing protocol it likes inside itself. That split gives two families of protocol with genuinely different goals. An **interior** protocol such as OSPF optimises a metric: everyone inside the AS is on the same side, so shortest path is a coherent thing to want, and link state plus areas delivers it.

An **exterior** protocol optimises nothing of the sort. **BGP** is a path-vector protocol: an announcement carries the full list of AS numbers the route traverses, which lets a receiver drop any path already containing its own AS - loop prevention with no metric and no map. What BGP then does with the surviving paths is **policy**, and the policy is commercial. A route learned from a customer earns money and is preferred; a route from a settlement-free peer is free; a route from a transit provider costs money and is the last resort. An AS will happily install a five-hop customer path over a two-hop provider path, so BGP's choices are frequently not the shortest ones and were never trying to be.

**ICMP** is IP's own error and diagnostic channel, carried inside IP with protocol number 1. It reports; it never fixes. A router discarding a datagram whose TTL reached zero sends **Time Exceeded** (type 11); an undeliverable datagram gets **Destination Unreachable** (type 3). Each error quotes the failed datagram's header and its first 8 bytes, so the sender can identify the connection at fault.

**Ping** is the simplest use: Echo Request (type 8) out, Echo Reply (type 0) back. **Traceroute** is cleverer, and is really TTL turned into an instrument. Send a probe with TTL 1 and the first router reports itself by expiring it; send TTL 2 and the second router does; walk the TTL upward and each expiry names the router at that distance, until a reply of a different kind says the destination itself has been reached. Because it depends on routers volunteering ICMP errors, a row of asterisks means a silent router, not a broken path.
sections.code:
$ traceroute -n 203.0.113.9
traceroute to 203.0.113.9, 30 hops max, 60 byte packets
 1  10.20.96.1     0.412 ms   0.398 ms   0.401 ms
 2  10.0.0.9       1.104 ms   1.087 ms   1.121 ms
 3  203.0.113.1    8.442 ms   8.501 ms   8.470 ms
 4  * * *
 5  203.0.113.9   14.203 ms  14.118 ms  14.190 ms

  hop 1   sent with TTL 1; the first router decremented it to 0,
          discarded it and returned ICMP type 11, Time Exceeded
  hop 4   the router at that distance answered nothing: it either does
          not generate ICMP errors or something filters them. The path
          is fine - hop 5 replied - so this is a silence, not a break
  hop 5   the destination itself, which answers differently: ICMP type
          3 Destination Unreachable, or an Echo Reply, depending on the
          probe. That different answer is how traceroute knows to stop

  ICMP types worth knowing
     0   Echo Reply                the second half of ping
     3   Destination Unreachable   code 3 is "port unreachable"
     8   Echo Request              the first half of ping
    11   Time Exceeded             TTL hit zero in transit

  Every ICMP error carries the offending datagram's IP header plus its
  first 8 bytes - enough to expose the TCP or UDP port numbers, so the
  sending host can work out which of its connections is being complained
  about rather than merely which of its machines.

annotations.text: Three probes per TTL value, which is why each row shows three times. Traceroute is sampling a path that may well change between probes.
Asterisks are the commonest misreading on this floor. A later hop answering proves the datagrams got through the silent one.
Eight bytes is exactly enough for a TCP or UDP source and destination port plus a sequence number, which is the minimum needed to name a connection rather than a host.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill in the four numbers. All four are ICMP types or TTL values.
checkpoint.template:
Ping sends ICMP type ___ and expects type ___ in reply.
A router discarding a datagram whose TTL reached zero sends ICMP type ___.
To make the fifth router on the path report itself, traceroute sets the TTL to ___.
checkpoint.explain: Echo Request is 8 and Echo Reply is 0, and it is worth noticing that the reply carries the smaller number - guessing that request and reply are 0 and 1, or 8 and 9, is the usual slip. Time Exceeded is 11, and since each router on the way decrements the TTL once, a TTL of n expires at the nth router, so the fifth router needs a TTL of exactly 5.

header-drills.prompt:
Parse this IPv4 header, byte for byte.

`45 00 00 3c 1c 46 40 00 40 06 9c bc c0 a8 00 68 c0 a8 00 01`

steps.label: header length in bytes
total length in bytes
payload length in bytes
identification, in decimal
is the DF flag set? yes or no
TTL
protocol, by name
destination address, dotted quad

header-drills.explain: `45` splits into version 4 and IHL 5, and IHL counts 32-bit words, so the header is 5 x 4 = 20 bytes; Total Length `003c` is 60 and counts the header too, leaving 40 bytes of payload. `4000` is the flags-and-offset word: the top three bits are 010, so DF is set and MF is clear, with an offset of zero. Reading `4000` as an offset of 16,384 is the trap - the offset is only the low thirteen bits, and here it is zero.

header-drills.prompt: A 1500-byte datagram with a 20-byte header, identification 7238 and `DF` clear must cross a link whose MTU is 576 bytes. Fragment it and report the results.

steps.label: largest payload one fragment may carry, in bytes
number of fragments produced
fragment 1 total length field
fragment 2 fragment offset field
fragment 3 total length field
fragment 3 MF flag, 0 or 1
identification field carried by fragment 3
which node reassembles the datagram: router or destination

header-drills.explain: The link allows 576 - 20 = 556 bytes of payload, but every offset counts 8-byte blocks, so the payload must round down to 552 and only the last fragment may be a non-multiple of 8. That gives 552 + 552 + 376 = 1480 bytes of payload in three pieces, with total lengths 572, 572 and 396 once each header is added back, and offsets of 0, 552/8 = 69 and 1104/8 = 138. Using 556 rather than 552 is the tempting arithmetic and it produces an offset that cannot be represented at all.

header-drills.prompt: The middle fragment from the previous problem - total length 572, identification 7238, fragment offset 69, `MF` set - now reaches a router whose outgoing link has an MTU of 300 bytes. Fragment it again.

steps.label: largest payload each new piece may carry, in bytes
number of pieces produced
piece 1 total length field
piece 1 fragment offset field
piece 2 fragment offset field
piece 2 MF flag, 0 or 1
identification field carried by both pieces

header-drills.explain: A fragment is refragmented exactly like any other datagram, except that its offsets are relative to the original payload, so the first piece keeps offset 69 and the second starts at 69 + 280/8 = 69 + 35 = 104. The MF flag on the last piece is the part people get wrong: this fragment already had MF set, so both pieces must keep it set - clearing it would tell the destination the datagram ends 376 bytes early, and the reassembly would silently truncate.

header-drills.prompt: The IPv4 header checksum is recomputed by every router the datagram passes through, and it protects the header only. Explain both facts: what forces the recomputation, and why leaving the data out of it is a deliberate choice rather than an oversight.
header-drills.explain: The TTL changes at every single hop, so any checksum covering it is stale the instant a router touches it - the recomputation is forced by IP's own bookkeeping, not by the network being unreliable. Leaving the payload out keeps that per-hop cost proportional to the header rather than to the data, and end-to-end integrity is a job the transport layer already does with its own checksum over the whole segment. The tempting objection, that IP is therefore not protecting the data, is correct and is the point: a check the routers redo constantly should be as small as possible, which is also why IPv6 removed the header checksum altogether.

forwarding-and-probing.prompt:
Use R1's forwarding table from the lesson and give the outgoing interface for each destination. The table is:

- `0.0.0.0/0` to eth0
- `10.0.0.0/8` to eth1
- `10.20.0.0/16` to eth2
- `10.20.64.0/18` to eth3
- `10.20.96.0/19` to eth4
- `192.168.4.0/24` to eth5
- `192.168.4.128/26` to eth6
forwarding-and-probing.explain: The two pairs are the whole exercise. 10.20.80.5 and 10.20.100.7 both sit inside the /18, which spans 10.20.64.0 to 10.20.127.255, but only the second is inside the /19, which starts at 10.20.96.0 - so one leaves by eth3 and the other by eth4. Likewise the /26 covers 192.168.4.128 to 192.168.4.191 exactly, so .191 takes eth6 and .192 falls back to the /24 and takes eth5. Off-by-one at a prefix boundary is the defect that never shows up in testing, because the boundary address is rarely the one anybody pings.

forwarding-and-probing.prompt: Prefix arithmetic on two of R1's entries. Give the count as a plain number and the addresses as dotted quads.
forwarding-and-probing.template:
`10.20.64.0/18` has netmask ___ and its last address is ___.
`192.168.4.128/26` covers ___ addresses, the last of which is ___.
forwarding-and-probing.explain: An /18 fixes eighteen bits, so the mask is 255.255.192.0 and the free bits run the third octet from 64 up to 127 - not to 191, which is where the next /18 would start. A /26 leaves 6 free bits, so 2^6 = 64 addresses beginning at .128 and ending at .128 + 63 = .191. Counting the block as 2^(32 - prefix) rather than trying to reason in octets is the habit that makes these instant.

forwarding-and-probing.prompt: A colleague says a router 'routes each packet as it arrives'. Correct them precisely: separate forwarding from routing, say what data each one touches and on what timescale each runs, and describe what a router does during the minutes after its routing protocol has crashed but its table is still in memory.
forwarding-and-probing.explain: Forwarding is a purely local operation on one packet against a table that already exists: match the destination, pick the next hop, decrement TTL, transmit. Routing is the distributed background process that writes that table, and it involves neighbours, timers and convergence. The crashed-protocol case is the clean test of whether the distinction has landed - the router keeps forwarding at full speed on a table that is quietly going stale, sending packets confidently down paths that may no longer exist, which is precisely why a silent routing failure is harder to notice than a dead interface.

forwarding-and-probing.prompt: An operator wants all traffic for `10.20.0.0/16` to leave R1 by eth2, and adds exactly that entry. It appears in the table and eth2 is up. Traffic to 10.20.200.1 does leave by eth2 as intended, but traffic to 10.20.100.7 keeps leaving by eth4 and traffic to 10.20.80.5 keeps leaving by eth3. Nothing is dropped and no error is logged. Name the cause and say what the operator must actually do.
forwarding-and-probing.answer: Longest-prefix match: the more specific /18 and /19 entries still cover those addresses and outrank the new /16
forwarding-and-probing.explain: The /16 is doing exactly what it was told to do: it catches every 10.20 address that no longer prefix already claims, which is why 10.20.200.1 obeys it and the others do not. A /16 cannot override a /18 or a /19, no matter where it sits in the table or when it was added, so the fix is to remove or repoint the more specific entries rather than to add anything. The tempting diagnosis is a broken or mis-ordered table - but a table with no ordering semantics cannot be mis-ordered, and the absence of drops and errors is itself the clue that forwarding is working perfectly.

forwarding-and-probing.prompt: Host H sends to server S along the path `H - R1 - R2 - R3 - R4 - S`, with an initial TTL of 64. Every router on the path generates ICMP errors normally.

steps.label: TTL in the datagram as it leaves R1
TTL in the datagram as it arrives at S
TTL H must set for R3 to be the node that discards the probe
ICMP type R3 returns in that case
which node discards a probe sent with TTL 4
ICMP type S returns to a ping Echo Request
how many distinct TTL values traceroute needs to name every node from R1 to S

forwarding-and-probing.explain: Each router decrements once before forwarding, so four routers cost four: 64 leaves H, 63 leaves R1, and 60 arrives at S. A probe with TTL n therefore dies at the nth router, which makes the mapping between TTL and hop number exactly one-to-one and is the entire mechanism of traceroute. Naming R1 through R4 plus S needs TTLs 1 to 5 - answering 4 is the usual slip, and it forgets that the destination itself has to be reached and answer differently before traceroute knows to stop.

routing-protocols.prompt:
Run Dijkstra from node `A` on this network. The links are undirected, and their costs are:

- `A-B` 4
- `A-C` 2
- `A-E` 9
- `B-C` 1
- `B-D` 5
- `C-D` 8
- `C-E` 10
- `D-E` 2
- `D-F` 6
- `E-F` 3

steps.label: second node confirmed, after A
third node confirmed
fourth node confirmed
final cost from A to B
final cost from A to D
final cost from A to E
final cost from A to F
A's next hop for traffic to D
A's next hop for traffic to F

routing-protocols.explain: B is reached more cheaply through C than directly - 2 + 1 = 3 beats the direct 4 - and that indirect route is what then makes D cost 3 + 5 = 8 rather than the 2 + 8 = 10 of the direct C-D link. E is the opposite case: the direct A-E link at 9 beats going round through D at 8 + 2 = 10, so F costs 9 + 3 = 12 and A's next hop for F is E, not C. Reading a next hop off the cost alone is the mistake to avoid; the next hop is the first edge of the whole path, which is why two destinations of similar cost can leave by different interfaces.

routing-protocols.prompt: `X --1-- Y --1-- Z` runs a distance-vector protocol with RIP's infinity of 16, and has converged on routes to X: Y's cost is 1, Z's is 2. The `X-Y` link then fails. Trace what happens with split horizon off, then answer the last step with split horizon on at Z.

steps.label: Y's cost to X after exchange 1
Y's next hop to X after exchange 1
Z's cost to X after exchange 2
Y's cost to X after exchange 3
by how much a cost rises per exchange
the cost at which X is finally declared unreachable
with split horizon on at Z, Y's cost to X after exchange 1

routing-protocols.explain: Y loses its direct link and takes the only offer on the table, Z's stale advertisement of 2, giving 1 + 2 = 3 through Z - a route that runs back through Y itself. Neither router can see that, because a distance vector carries a number and a next hop and no trace of the path, so each new advertisement is believed and the pair ratchet upward one at a time until they reach the deliberately small infinity of 16. Split horizon removes the offer entirely: Z learned its route to X from Y, so it never mentions X to Y, Y finds nothing to fall back on, and the route goes to infinity in a single exchange.

routing-protocols.prompt: State the split horizon rule precisely, say what poison reverse adds to it, and then explain why neither of them stops a routing loop that runs round three routers. Be concrete about what a router can and cannot see.
routing-protocols.explain: Split horizon says: do not advertise a route back out of the interface you learned it from. Poison reverse advertises it back with a cost of infinity instead of staying silent, which is stronger because it actively overwrites a stale entry rather than waiting for one to time out. Both address only the two-router case, because both work by recognising the one neighbour a route came from - and in a loop A to B to C to A, nobody is advertising a route straight back to the router it learned it from, so every advertisement looks legitimate. The underlying reason is that a distance vector carries no path, which is exactly the information BGP adds to solve the same problem outright.

routing-protocols.prompt: Put the steps of a link-state protocol reacting to a failure into the order they happen.
fragments: a link attached to router R fails, and R notices
R builds a link-state packet listing its remaining neighbours and the cost to each, stamped with a fresh sequence number
R floods that packet out of every one of its interfaces
each receiving router compares the sequence number, stores the packet only if it is newer, and floods it onward
flooding settles, and every router in the area holds the same map of the topology
each router independently runs Dijkstra over that map, rooted at itself
each router installs, for every destination, the first hop of its own shortest-path tree
routing-protocols.explain: The sequence-number check sits inside the flooding step, not after it: without it the packet would circulate forever, since flooding has no other stopping rule. Note also that the computation is the last thing to happen and is entirely local - no router tells another what the shortest path is, they simply all run the same algorithm on the same map and therefore agree. Putting Dijkstra before the flooding settles is the tempting order, and it produces exactly the transient loops that fast flooding exists to shorten.

routing-protocols.prompt: You operate AS 64500, a regional ISP. AS 64501 is a customer that pays you; AS 64502 is a settlement-free peer; AS 64503 is your transit provider, whom you pay. All three announce a route to the same prefix, and the path through your provider is the shortest in AS hops. Say which route you install and why, which of your neighbours you re-advertise it to, and what would go wrong if you re-advertised your peer's routes to your provider. Then say why you would still run OSPF and not BGP inside AS 64500.
routing-protocols.explain: You install the customer route even though it is the longest, because that is the one you are paid to carry, and BGP's local preference exists precisely so that commercial ranking can override AS-path length. Customer routes are re-advertised to everybody; peer and provider routes are re-advertised only to customers, because announcing a peer's route to your provider tells the world you will carry traffic between two networks that pay you nothing - free transit that you would then have to buy. Inside the AS the situation is completely different: there is one administrative owner, no policy to express and no trust boundary, so an interior protocol optimising a metric is the right tool, and OSPF's areas keep the flooding and the shortest-path computation bounded as the network grows.

exam.prompt: The `Fragment Offset` field of an IPv4 header is measured in units of:
choices: single bytes
8-byte blocks
32-bit words
the MTU of the outgoing link
exam.explain: The field is only 13 bits, which as a byte count would reach 8,191; counting 8-byte blocks stretches that to 65,528 and so covers any legal datagram. The 32-bit answer is the tempting one because IHL really does count 32-bit words, but the two fields use different units for entirely different reasons.

exam.prompt: A router discards a datagram because its TTL reached zero. Which ICMP message does it send back?
choices: type 0, Echo Reply
type 3, Destination Unreachable
type 8, Echo Request
type 11, Time Exceeded
exam.explain: Time Exceeded, type 11, is the message traceroute lives on. Destination Unreachable is the tempting alternative because the datagram indeed never arrived, but type 3 means the router could find no way onward at all, which is a different failure from a datagram that ran out of hops on a perfectly good path.

exam.prompt: Complete the four header limits. Give every answer as a plain number.
exam.template:
IHL counts ___-byte words, so the largest legal IPv4 header is ___ bytes.
Total Length is ___ bits wide, capping a whole datagram at ___ bytes.
exam.explain: IHL is four bits, so its largest value is 15, and 15 words of 4 bytes is 60 - which is why IPv4 options are limited to 40 bytes. Total Length is 16 bits and counts the header as well as the payload, so 65,535 is the size of the whole datagram and not of the data alone.

exam.prompt: Put what a router does to one datagram into the order it does it.
fragments: verify the header checksum, and discard the datagram silently if it fails
look the destination up in the forwarding table, longest prefix winning
decrement the TTL, and if it is now zero discard the datagram and return ICMP Time Exceeded
fragment the datagram if the outgoing link's MTU is too small and DF is clear
recompute the header checksum, since the TTL and possibly the length have changed
hand the datagram to the outgoing link
exam.explain: The checksum brackets everything: verified before the router changes anything, recomputed after it has changed the TTL and possibly the total length. The lookup has to precede fragmentation because it is the lookup that reveals which link the datagram is leaving and therefore which MTU applies - fragmenting first would mean fragmenting to a size nobody asked for.

exam.prompt: TTL arithmetic. A host whose operating system uses an initial TTL of 64 receives a reply carrying TTL 57. Separately, a routing loop of exactly four routers has formed, and a datagram enters it having just been sent with TTL 64.

steps.label: how many routers the reply crossed
TTL the reply carried as it left the last router before the host
how many complete laps of the four-router loop the datagram makes
TTL when the datagram is finally discarded

exam.explain: Each router decrements once, so 64 - 57 = 7 routers, and the value the host sees is by definition the value the last router sent. Round the loop, four routers cost 4 per lap, so 64 / 4 = 16 laps take the TTL to exactly 0 and the sixteenth lap is where it dies. It is worth noticing what TTL actually bought here: not prevention of the loop, which is the routing protocol's job, but a hard bound on how long one datagram can suffer from it.

exam.prompt:
A different router has this forwarding table. Give the outgoing interface for each destination.

- `0.0.0.0/0` to eth0
- `172.16.0.0/12` to eth1
- `172.16.128.0/17` to eth2
- `172.16.130.0/24` to eth3
exam.explain: 172.16.131.1 is the instructive one: it is inside the /17, which runs from 172.16.128.0 to 172.16.255.255, but one octet outside the /24, which stops at 172.16.130.255. The /12 spans 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255, so 172.31.255.254 is very nearly its last address and still matches, while 172.32.0.1 lies beyond it and falls to the default. Assuming a /12 covers all of 172.x is the trap - it covers sixteen values of the second octet, not all 256.

exam.prompt: Compare distance vector and link state. Say what each router has to know, what each has to send and how often, how each computes its table, and give the characteristic failure mode of each. Finish by saying which one you would deploy in an AS of eight hundred routers, and why.
exam.explain: Distance vector stores one cost per destination and sends that whole vector to its neighbours only; link state stores the entire topology and floods a small packet about its own links to everyone. The computation mirrors that: Bellman-Ford incrementally on received vectors, versus Dijkstra run locally over a map every router agrees on. Their failure modes are mirror images too - distance vector converges slowly and wrongly through count-to-infinity, while link state converges fast but at the cost of memory, flooding traffic and a full recomputation on every change. At eight hundred routers link state with areas is the usual answer, because bounded flooding scales better than unbounded slow convergence, and slow convergence is the failure a large network cannot tolerate.

exam.prompt: Ping to 198.51.100.20 succeeds with one per cent loss and a steady 42 ms round trip. Traceroute to the very same address names hops 1 to 4, then prints only asterisks for hops 5, 6, 7 and 8, and then names 198.51.100.20 itself at hop 9. Bulk transfers to the host are also fine. Name the cause and say what, if anything, is broken.
exam.answer: The routers at those hops are not returning ICMP Time Exceeded - suppressed, rate-limited or filtered - while forwarding normally
exam.explain: Hop 9 answering is the proof: datagrams passed through hops 5 to 8 intact, so those routers forwarded perfectly and merely declined to generate the ICMP Time Exceeded messages traceroute depends on. Routers commonly rate-limit or suppress ICMP errors and firewalls commonly discard them, so a block of asterisks in the middle of a path that completes is normal and not a fault. The tempting diagnosis is packet loss in the middle of the path, but loss there would degrade the ping and the bulk transfers too, and both are healthy.

sections.title: The demultiplexor, and the freedom to promise nothing
sections.body:
IP delivers a datagram to a **host**. It has no idea that a host runs hundreds of processes, and no field that could say which one. The transport layer's irreducible job is therefore **demultiplexing**: adding a **port** number so the receiving kernel can hand the payload to the right socket. Everything else transport does is optional, and **UDP** is the protocol that takes that word seriously.

UDP adds eight bytes - source port, destination port, length, checksum - and stops. There is no handshake, no acknowledgement, no retransmission, no ordering, no duplicate suppression and no rate control. The checksum detects corruption and then discards the datagram silently; UDP will tell you a datagram was wrong only by never delivering it. A UDP socket is identified by the pair `(destination IP, destination port)`, which is why two UDP sockets cannot share a port on the same address, while two TCP connections routinely share port 80 because TCP demultiplexes on the full four-tuple.

The absence of guarantees is not a deficiency to be apologised for; for some traffic it is the correct engineering. DNS asks one question and gets one answer: building a connection to carry 60 bytes costs an extra round trip before the query even leaves, and if the reply is lost the resolver can simply ask again. Real-time voice is stronger still - a packet that arrives after its playout deadline is worthless, so retransmitting it wastes bandwidth **and** delays the packets behind it. QUIC runs over UDP for a third reason: it wants to implement reliability itself, in user space, where it can be changed without waiting a decade for every kernel on Earth.

The cost is real and falls on the application. It must tolerate loss, reordering and duplication, and - the part people forget - it must not flood the network, because nothing in UDP will slow it down when the network is in trouble. Overhead is the small consolation: on a 30-byte payload over IPv4, UDP spends 58 bytes on the wire against TCP's 70, so 51.7% of the packet is payload rather than 42.9%.
sections.code:
UDP header - eight bytes, and every one of them earns its place.

  0                   16                  31
 +--------------------+--------------------+
 |    Source port     |  Destination port  |
 +--------------------+--------------------+
 |       Length       |      Checksum      |
 +--------------------+--------------------+
 |                Payload                  |
 +-----------------------------------------+

Demultiplexing keys, and they are not the same shape:

  UDP socket   ->  (destination IP, destination port)
  TCP socket   ->  (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port)

So two TCP connections can share port 80 on one host and still be told
apart, while two UDP sockets cannot share a port unless one is connected.

Overhead on a 30-byte payload, over IPv4:

  UDP:  20 (IP) +  8 (UDP) + 30 = 58 bytes,  51.7% payload
  TCP:  20 (IP) + 20 (TCP) + 30 = 70 bytes,  42.9% payload

annotations.text: The source port is what makes a reply possible at all. It is the only place a receiver learns where to send the answer, and it is why an unconnected UDP socket still has to have one.

The checksum covers the payload and a pseudo-header taken from the IP header, so a datagram delivered to the wrong address is caught too. A failed checksum causes a silent discard - no error is ever reported to anybody.
Four fields, not two. This is the whole reason a web server can hold ten thousand simultaneous connections on one port: the connections differ in the client's address and port, not in the server's.

Twelve bytes of difference per packet. On a voice stream sending fifty 30-byte frames a second that is 4.8 kb/s, which mattered enormously when the access link was a modem and matters not at all today.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete the facts that separate the two transport protocols at their narrowest point.
checkpoint.template:
A UDP socket is demultiplexed on the destination IP address and the destination ___ .
A TCP socket is demultiplexed on all ___ fields of the connection.
The UDP header is ___ bytes long; the minimum TCP header is 20.
When UDP's checksum fails, the datagram is ___ and nobody is told.
checkpoint.explain: The two-tuple against four-tuple difference is the one with practical consequences: it decides whether two conversations can share a port, and it is why a TCP server needs only one listening port for every client in the world. The silent discard is the other thing worth remembering - UDP has a checksum but no error report, so an application that needs to know about corruption has to notice the gap in its own data.

sections.title: Opening in three messages, closing in four
sections.body:
A TCP connection is a shared numbering agreement, and the **three-way handshake** exists to establish it in both directions. The client sends a SYN carrying its **initial sequence number** $x$; the server replies with a SYN of its own carrying $y$ and an acknowledgement of $x + 1$; the client acknowledges $y + 1$. Two messages would be enough to tell the server the client's number, but nothing would confirm the server's, so three is the minimum that leaves both sides certain their own number was heard.

The `+ 1` is not decoration. SYN and FIN each **consume one sequence number** even though they carry no data, which is what lets them be acknowledged, retransmitted and ordered like any other byte. Initial sequence numbers are chosen unpredictably rather than starting at zero, partly so that a delayed segment from a previous connection between the same two ports cannot be mistaken for current data, and partly so an off-path attacker cannot guess a valid sequence number and inject into somebody else's connection.

Closing takes four messages because a TCP connection is two independent byte streams and each is shut down separately. A **FIN** means only **I have no more data to send**, and the peer may keep sending for as long as it likes - this is the **half-close**, and it is exactly what a shell pipeline needs when a client finishes its input and waits for output. The peer's TCP acknowledges the FIN immediately, but its own FIN cannot be sent until its **application** calls close, and the gap between those two events is the `CLOSE_WAIT` state. A host accumulating thousands of sockets in `CLOSE_WAIT` has an application bug, not a network problem.

The side that closes first ends in **`TIME_WAIT`** and stays there for twice the maximum segment lifetime - two minutes if MSL is 60 seconds - which strikes everyone as excessive until they see what it buys. It absorbs a delayed duplicate from the dying connection so that a new connection reusing the same four-tuple cannot be poisoned by it, and it keeps the final ACK's sender alive to retransmit if that ACK is lost, because the peer sitting in `LAST_ACK` has no other way to be released.
sections.code:
Three-way handshake. Client ISN = 3000, server ISN = 9000.

  client                                          server
    |  SYN  seq=3000                                 |
    | ---------------------------------------------> |
    |                      SYN,ACK seq=9000 ack=3001 |
    | <--------------------------------------------- |
    |  ACK  seq=3001 ack=9001                        |
    | ---------------------------------------------> |
    |                                                |

SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number, which is why the
acknowledgement of a bare SYN is ISN + 1 with no data sent at all.

Four-way close, the client closing first, after sending 4000 bytes
and receiving 7000:

  client                                          server
 ESTABLISHED |  FIN seq=4001 ack=7001             | ESTABLISHED
 FIN_WAIT_1  | --------------------------------->  |
             |            ACK ack=4002             | CLOSE_WAIT
 FIN_WAIT_2  | <---------------------------------  |
             |       FIN seq=7001 ack=4002         | LAST_ACK
             | <---------------------------------  |
 TIME_WAIT   |  ACK ack=7002                       |
             | --------------------------------->  | CLOSED
 (2 x MSL)   |                                     |
 CLOSED      |                                     |

annotations.text: One segment doing two jobs: it acknowledges the client's SYN and carries the server's own. That packing is why the handshake is three messages rather than four.
Acknowledging 3001 when byte 3001 does not exist yet is the giveaway. The ACK field always names the next byte expected, and the SYN occupied number 3000.

The server's TCP acknowledges the FIN at once, but its own FIN waits on the application. Everything between here and LAST_ACK is CLOSE_WAIT, and a heap of sockets stuck there means somebody never called close.
Two full segment lifetimes of doing nothing. It is the price of guaranteeing that no stale duplicate of this connection can still be wandering the network when the same four-tuple is reused.

checkpoint.prompt: Put the segments and state changes of a connection's opening and its close into the order they occur. The client opens the connection and also closes it first.
fragments: the client sends SYN with its own initial sequence number and nothing else
the server replies with a single segment carrying its own SYN and an ACK of the client's ISN + 1
the client acknowledges the server's ISN + 1 and the connection is ESTABLISHED in both directions
the client sends FIN and enters FIN_WAIT_1, promising no further data of its own
the server's TCP acknowledges that FIN and the server socket sits in CLOSE_WAIT while its application still holds the socket open
the server's application calls close, its FIN goes out and it enters LAST_ACK
the client acknowledges that FIN and waits out 2 x MSL in TIME_WAIT
checkpoint.explain: The step people misplace is the fifth: the ACK of a FIN and the peer's own FIN are two separate segments separated by an unbounded amount of time, because only the application can decide it has finished sending. Collapsing them into one exchange gives a symmetric four-message close that would be wrong - it would make a FIN mean the whole connection is over, and the half-close would become impossible.

sections.title: Cumulative acknowledgements, and knowing when to give up waiting
sections.body:
TCP numbers **bytes**, not segments, and its acknowledgement field names the next byte the receiver expects. That single choice makes every ACK **cumulative**: an ACK of 1501 asserts that everything up to and including byte 1500 arrived, so a lost ACK is repaired by the next one to get through, and the receiver never has to track which acknowledgements the sender actually saw. The price is that the acknowledgement cannot step over a hole. If one segment is lost, the receiver may buffer everything that follows it, but every ACK it sends keeps naming the same missing byte - which is why the SACK option was added, to describe the blocks that **did** arrive alongside the cumulative number.

A sender therefore retransmits on one of two triggers. The first is a **timeout**, and choosing its length is the hard part. Too short and the sender retransmits segments that were merely slow, wasting capacity exactly when the network is already struggling; too long and a lost segment stalls the connection for a period the user notices. The timeout must track the round-trip time, which varies by orders of magnitude across paths and by a factor of ten on one path as queues fill.

Jacobson and Karels' answer smooths both the mean and the variation: with $\alpha = 1/8$ and $\beta = 1/4$, each new sample updates $DevRTT$ and $EstimatedRTT$, and the timer is set to $EstimatedRTT + 4 \times DevRTT$. The deviation term is what makes it work - on a steady path the timeout hugs the estimate, and on a jittery one it stands well clear, without anyone tuning a constant per path. **Karn's algorithm** adds the rule that saves it from feedback: never take an RTT sample from a segment that was retransmitted, because you cannot tell whether the ACK answers the original or the copy, and instead double the timeout on each successive expiry.

Waiting for a timer is still slow, and a duplicate ACK is evidence that arrived far sooner. If the receiver keeps repeating the same acknowledgement, segments **are** getting through - just not the one that matters. **Fast retransmit** treats the third duplicate ACK as sufficient proof of loss and resends immediately, without waiting for the timer. Three rather than one, because reordering in the network produces one or two duplicates routinely and mistaking mild reordering for loss would make TCP retransmit constantly.
sections.code:
Cumulative acknowledgement. Segments of 500 bytes from seq 1001;
the second one is lost.

  sent   1001-1500  ->  ACK 1501
  sent   1501-2000  ->  LOST
  sent   2001-2500  ->  ACK 1501   (duplicate 1)
  sent   2501-3000  ->  ACK 1501   (duplicate 2)
  sent   3001-3500  ->  ACK 1501   (duplicate 3)  -> fast retransmit
  resend 1501-2000  ->  ACK 3501

The retransmission timer, Jacobson and Karels, alpha = 1/8, beta = 1/4:

  DevRTT       = (1 - beta)  * DevRTT       + beta  * |Sample - EstRTT|
  EstimatedRTT = (1 - alpha) * EstimatedRTT + alpha * Sample
  Timeout      = EstimatedRTT + 4 * DevRTT

Karn: never take a sample from a segment that was retransmitted - the
ACK is ambiguous - and double the timeout on each successive expiry.

annotations.text: The receiver has segment 2001-2500 in hand and cannot say so with the cumulative field alone. All it can do is repeat 1501, which is simultaneously an acknowledgement and a complaint.

One ACK jumps from 1501 to 3501 because the hole is now filled and the cumulative number is free to run forward over everything already buffered. That single jump is the payoff for the three preceding duplicates.

Four deviations, not two or one: TCP would rather wait too long occasionally than retransmit a segment that was only delayed, because a spurious retransmission adds load to a path that is already the reason for the delay.

The ambiguity is genuine and unfixable by measurement: an ACK for byte 1501 looks identical whether it answers the original or the copy, so a sample taken here can be wrong by an entire timeout period.

checkpoint.prompt: A sender transmits three 400-byte segments starting at sequence number 5001, back to back. The **first** one is lost; the other two arrive and are buffered. Give the acknowledgement number in each ACK the receiver sends, and then the ACK sent after the lost segment is retransmitted.

steps.label: ACK sent when segment 2 (5401-5800) arrives
ACK sent when segment 3 (5801-6200) arrives
ACK sent after segment 1 (5001-5400) is retransmitted and arrives
bytes the receiver held out of order before that last ACK

checkpoint.explain: The receiver cannot acknowledge 5801 or 6201 while byte 5001 is missing, because a cumulative ACK claims everything below it. The tempting answers are 5801 and 6201 for the first two steps - that is what a selective acknowledgement would say, and it is precisely the information the cumulative field is unable to carry, which is why SACK had to be bolted on as an option.

sections.title: One sliding window, doing two different jobs
sections.body:
A sender that transmits one segment and waits for its ACK achieves one segment per round trip, which on a fast long path is derisory. The **sliding window** lets it keep several segments in flight at once, and the window's size is the amount of unacknowledged data allowed: $LastByteSent - LastByteAcked \le AdvertisedWindow$. The **effective window** - what may go out right now - is that limit minus what is already outstanding, and it opens again only when an ACK arrives and slides the left edge forward.

The receiver sets the limit, in every ACK, from the space left in its buffer: $AdvertisedWindow = RcvBuffer - (LastByteRcvd - LastByteRead)$. This is **flow control**, and it protects exactly one thing - the receiver's memory. An application that stops reading fills the buffer, the advertised window shrinks towards zero, and the sender stops. Note what it does **not** protect: the routers in between have no say in this number at all, and a receiver with a huge buffer will happily advertise more than the path can carry. Protecting the network is congestion control, a separate mechanism with a separate window, and conflating the two is the commonest confusion in transport.

A zero window creates a deadlock that TCP has to break by hand. The sender is blocked, so it will send nothing; the window update, when the application finally reads, rides on a pure ACK - and pure ACKs are not retransmitted, so if that one is lost the connection stops forever. The sender therefore runs a **persist timer** and sends periodic one-byte zero-window probes, which force the receiver to reply with its current window. The related **silly window syndrome** is the receiver announcing a 1-byte opening the moment a byte is read, provoking a 41-byte packet to carry it; the cure is to withhold the update until the window is worth advertising.

The window is also the ceiling on throughput, whatever the link is capable of: $Throughput \le Window / RTT$. On a 1 Gb/s path with an 80 ms round trip the **bandwidth-delay product** is 10,000,000 bytes, and the largest window the 16-bit header field can express, 65,535 bytes, yields 819,187.5 bytes per second - 6.5535 Mb/s, or 0.66% of the link. That is why the window-scale option exists, negotiated in the handshake, shifting the field left by up to 14 places. Widening the window then exposes the next limit: the sequence space is 32 bits, and at 1 Gb/s it wraps in 34.36 seconds, which is what timestamps were added to disambiguate.
sections.code:
Receiver, with a 4000-byte receive buffer:

  AdvertisedWindow = RcvBuffer - (LastByteRcvd - LastByteRead)

Sender, obeying it:

  LastByteSent - LastByteAcked  <=  AdvertisedWindow
  EffectiveWindow = AdvertisedWindow - (LastByteSent - LastByteAcked)

Ceiling on throughput, whatever the link can do:

  Throughput  <=  Window / RTT

  1 Gb/s, RTT 80 ms   ->  bandwidth-delay product 10,000,000 bytes
  65,535-byte window  ->  819,187.5 bytes/s
                       =  6.5535 Mb/s, 0.66% of the link

The window field is 16 bits, so the window-scale option shifts it left by
up to 14 places. The sequence space is 32 bits: at 1 Gb/s it wraps in
34.36 seconds, which is why the timestamp option exists.
